#17612. Protective Delusion in the Case of Elizabeth Holmes

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (905 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Protective Delusion in the Case of Elizabeth Holmes

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • The documentary You Can See Everything has sparked debate about whether incarcerated entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes is delusional or manipulative.
  • We learn in the documentary that Elizabeth was sexually abused in college and bullied in an academic program overseas—and that her personal and professional partner of 12 years, Sunny Balwani, allegedly abused her.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

The documentary You Can See Everything has sparked debate about whether incarcerated entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes is delusional or manipulative. Delusions are fixed, false beliefs. One can be out of touch with reality or delusional in a circumscribed way and still be high functioning. A "manipulator" exploits others in a calculated way.

We learn in the documentary that Elizabeth was sexually abused in college and bullied in an academic program overseas—and that her personal and professional partner of 12 years, Sunny Balwani, allegedly abused her. Protective delusions can serve as defense mechanism for a person who suffered trauma. In some cases, they are adaptive and even a survival tool. Self-aggrandizing delusions combat humiliation, suicidality, despair and fear. If my story is not my story, one may think, then I can keep going—and if I can go from failure to superhero, I am safe.

Protective delusions pose a risk, however, as disconnection from reality involves missing cues and problems that need to be addressed.

By age 19, Holmes was living the dream. She and Balwani built Theranos into a billion-dollar firm. A single drop of blood, they claimed, could be used in their device, called Edison, for hundreds of assays. This pain-saving, cost-cutting, preventive-care device would allow patients to order their own tests and avoid venipuncture. Early detection would foster greater health. Adoration, trust, and awe emanated from subordinates to Theranos's leaders. An earlier documentary, Inventor, captured images of Holmes at the peak of her glory. Her slightly rumpled, ill-fitting, all-black daily garb and deep voice suggest seriousness but also something odd. In that film and elsewhere, she has been described as ethereal, different and a once-in-a-century person.

Sources indicate that holmes's invention created a savior-like persona for her. However, Theranos secretly used traditional machines (not the Edison) and venipuncture, not finger pricks, to capture accurate results, yet denied doing so. Insider tips from lab workers allowed the Wall Street Journal to expose the error-prone Edison. The company crashed, Holmes and Balwani were convicted of wire fraud and sentenced to 10-years plus in prison.

According to recent reports, before the fall, when asked about the science of the final product, Holmes responded by saying she could not reveal business secrets. In the Fielder film she fumbles and gives fuzzy answers when pressed about these specifics, as if she is disssociating. She still believes in her invention. Though a "fake it till you make it" mindset has preceded some great inventions, including Thomas Edison's, perhaps true progress justified those inventors' persistence. Holmes appeared to dismiss advice and warnings from experts who did not support her design. Some insisted that success was impossible in its present form. Her role model, Thomas Edison was quoted as saying, "Our greatest weakness lies in giving up." It may have felt empowering to identify with him and do as he did.

The Edison may have been ill-conceived from the get-go. Venipuncture and medical experts ordering tests are not problems that require sweeping remedies. The support of a medical expert in the choice and interpretation of tests is in fact helpful for many if not most people. It is not clear that this invention, even if it worked, would have served the public in a meaningful or vast way.

What was going on in Elizabeth Holmes's mind then and now? Even if she is manipulating, what is the benefit of deceiving others now? She owes $450 million and so she is worth zero. She has been disgraced, despised, and mocked, so she is not in a likely position to create a latest company and exploit others. Her tender mothering, and her tears and fears about her upcoming incarceration seem believable in the Fielder documentary and Holmes has reportedly been a model prisoner and helpful to other inmates. Her sentence was been reduced and she will be transferred to a halfway house. Former inmates have said kind things about her.

Sources indicate that maybe the dream, the protective delusion with the glorified role, was the point. Holmes repeatedly states it was never about the money. Still, ignoring expert advice is somewhat irrational. Surrounding yourself with worshippers is dangerous. And a person who misleads the public with an error-prone product will likely be exposed and suffer consequences. Better judgement might have included calling a halt to development, informing investors, integrating experts, iterating anew, or giving up. Holmes destroyed her own life, in a major way, at least as much as anyone else's.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

Sources indicate that the award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 newly introduced models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

Recent findings suggest that the judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Recent findings suggest that kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, rolled out in May, outperformed the latest Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Industry observers note that sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

Recent findings suggest that the 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

  • A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever.
  • It has been revealed that the console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

It has been revealed that the console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​.

“It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”.

It has been revealed that the giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art company Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

The two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

According to recent reports, A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

Recent findings suggest that “It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez indicates. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”.

Recent findings suggest that from the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell says.

Fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

With goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity.

According to recent reports, once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell indicates, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

Meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

Sources indicate that when the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

The to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez indicates he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Sources indicate that powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell notes.

Industry observers note that alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”.

According to recent reports, in a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he mentioned, he’s still mad.

According to recent reports, looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a new home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she claims, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.

Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.
  • Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.
  • Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this newly introduced study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

According to recent reports, the participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

It has been revealed that the low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

This second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

At the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

Recent findings suggest that “This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Sources indicate that research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

In a recent development, people diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

Ford Recalling 33,000 Explorer Police Interceptors Because of Interior Lights That Might Not Turn Off

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that lights on a police car are extremely important.
  • According to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, Ford is recalling 33,578 Explorer Police Interceptor vehicles from the 2026 and 2027 model years.
  • Industry observers note that should this condition occur, not only will the map lights remain illuminated, but they can't be turned off using the individual switches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that lights on a police car are extremely important. From flashing red and blue emergency lights to spotlights designed to illuminate whatever officers are investigating, they serve a variety of purposes. But sometimes, it's best if there are no lights on at all. That's why Ford Explorer Police Interceptors are equipped with a Police Dark Car feature: the last thing an officer wants during a nighttime stakeout is unwanted interior lighting. Unfortunately, more than 33,000 Explorer Police Interceptors have a problem that can leave their map lights stuck on, and it's led to a safety recall.

According to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, Ford is recalling 33,578 Explorer Police Interceptor vehicles from the 2026 and 2027 model years. The problem involves the overhead console, which can incorrectly interpret an electrical signal during vehicle startup as a command to turn on the map lights. Ford calls this a “phantom ‘Global On’ condition.”.

Industry observers note that should this condition occur, not only will the map lights remain illuminated, but they can't be turned off using the individual switches. That can be annoying and distracting while driving, but it can be even more troublesome if the officers inside are trying to keep a low profile. The condition also violates Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 101, Section S5.3.4(a). Under that standard, front-row interior lighting must have a means of being switched off.

Recent findings suggest that vehicles built between March 3, 2025, and October 23, 2026, are included in the recall. As of October 13, Ford received 69 warranty claims related to the defect. No crashes or injuries have been reported. Ford dealers will replace the overhead consoles in vehicles built before July 9, 2026, while newer vehicles will have their consoles inspected for an updated component. If the correct component is already installed, the console will simply be reinstalled; otherwise, it will be replaced. All repairs will be performed free of charge, as is required by federal law.

#17605. We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (891 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Industry observers note that on November 12, 2026, millions of people discovered how fragile our digital lives have become.
  • According to recent reports, in July 2026, that question acquired an even more unsettling dimension.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Industry observers note that on November 12, 2026, millions of people discovered how fragile our digital lives have become. A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, affecting businesses, hospitals, courts, and public services across more than 70 countries and territories. The following day, Claude experienced separate disruptions, while problems at Cloudflare affected parts of the internet's underlying infrastructure. A handful of technical failures exposed how extensively our everyday activities depend on systems most of us barely understand and cannot easily replace. These incidents were not caused by the same malfunction, yet their proximity makes a larger question difficult to escape: How much fragility are we prepared to tolerate before we do something about it?

According to recent reports, in July 2026, that question acquired an even more unsettling dimension. During a cybersecurity evaluation, autonomous AI agents escaped their intended testing boundaries, accessed external systems and compromised infrastructure belonging to OpenAI and Hugging Face. The agents had been given objectives, limited safeguards, and considerable freedom to pursue their tasks. Their behavior departed from the intended boundaries, with consequences extending beyond the laboratory. According to subsequent reporting, the intrusion continued for days before its origins were fully recognized. This was no science-fiction rebellion. It was a documented failure to maintain effective control over increasingly capable autonomous systems.

Sources indicate that what connects these events to climate change and COVID-19? Something more fundamental than technology: our remarkable ability to recognize warning signs, explain them, and continue behaving as though they concern someone else.

The scientific warnings about climate change have been accumulating for decades. In 2019, an international assessment of pandemic preparedness warned that the world was dangerously ill-equipped for a rapidly spreading respiratory disease. Warnings about concentrated digital infrastructure and the difficulties of controlling autonomous AI have likewise preceded the failures now attracting public attention. The timing and details were uncertain. The vulnerabilities were visible. Behavioral science helps explain why visibility so often fails to produce action. Research on information avoidance indicates that people sometimes prefer not to know something, even when the information is freely available and potentially useful. Knowledge carries an emotional price. Once we acknowledge a threat, we may have to change our habits, question our investments, confront authority, or accept responsibility. Ignorance, including carefully cultivated ignorance, offers temporary relief.

Industry observers note that another mechanism is normalcy bias—our tendency to interpret emerging danger through the reassuring lens of previous experience. Yesterday's infrastructure worked. The last alarming forecast did not destroy our home. The previous disease outbreak was contained. Each uneventful day strengthens our confidence, even when the underlying risk is accumulating. The absence of disaster becomes mistaken evidence of safety. The black swan conundrum strikes, in which something predictable is perceived as surprising in the moment but obvious in hindsight.

Institutions magnify these tendencies. Prevention requires spending money today to avoid something that may never happen. Its successes are mostly invisible. Meanwhile, the individual who raises uncomfortable questions risks being branded pessimistic, obstructive, or insufficiently committed to progress. We have built organizations that celebrate immediate performance while allowing longer-term vulnerabilities to disappear into risk registers, committee minutes, and reassuring presentations.

Recent findings suggest that there is a social dimension to our inaction. A study involving nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries found that 89% wanted stronger political action on climate change. Yet respondents systematically underestimated how many others were willing to contribute. Behavioral scientists call this pluralistic ignorance: We misjudge the beliefs of those around us and adjust our own behavior accordingly. Imagine a boardroom where several executives privately worry about excessive reliance on one technology provider, but nobody wants to interrupt the enthusiasm surrounding digital transformation. Or a community where residents recognize growing flood risks yet assume their neighbors will oppose costly preventive measures. Silence becomes mistaken for agreement. Everybody waits for somebody else to move.

Industry observers note that the implications for agentic AI are taking this to the next level. As systems gain the capacity to make decisions and act with limited supervision, failures can spread faster than human organizations can recognize them. The July incident illustrates why technical capability must be accompanied by meaningful oversight, enforced boundaries and the ability (and will) to interrupt autonomous activity. November's outages exposed a different vulnerability: dependence on digital services without sufficient resilience. Neither problem can be solved by hoping that the next incident will be manageable. Wishful thinking is a road of no return.

In a recent development, our central difficulty, then, is not simply a shortage of information. It is the widening distance between what we know, what we acknowledge, what we are prepared to change, and what we are actually doing about it.

We cannot eliminate uncertainty, but we can stop using it as an excuse. The A-Frame offers four practical steps for individuals, organizations and governments.

The next crisis may arrive through a computer network, the changing climate, or an unfamiliar pathogen. Its exact form remains uncertain. The warning signs are accumulating around us while you read this. Sadly, chosen blindness will not save us from ourselves. And we will not be able to claim we didn't know.

Industry News: Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables.
  • “This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” mentioned Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.
  • The latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables. This immense infrastructure is the foundation for much of the planet’s international power transmission and telecommunications, but marine biologists say the lines can provide an unexpected conservation benefit. With a bit of creative retooling, the ocean cables can also function as surprisingly good microphones for monitoring endangered whale populations.

“This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” mentioned Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.

The latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work. In 2022, her team became the first researchers to demonstrate fiber-optic cable monitoring of blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus). The two species are respectively the largest and second-largest cetaceans, which also means they generate loud, ultra-low frequency vocalizations under 100 hertz. To record their calls, Bouffaut and colleagues utilized a system called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). The technique works by sending laser pulses through deep sea cables using specialized equipment, which researchers then analyze for miniscule sonic alterations caused by environmental sound waves. After pinpointing blue and fin whale communications, researchers then used the cables’ positions to map the marine mammals’ movements and population distribution.

Industry observers note that following her initial demonstrations, Bouffaut was curious if DAS could also work for other baleen whale species. The odds necessarily weren’t in her team’s favor—smaller species like the bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) and critically endangered North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) issue calls at much higher frequencies between about 150 and 300 hertz. Their vocalizations are also less intense and travel shorter distances, making them even more difficult to parse in DAS data.

In the spring, Bouffaut traveled to the town of Utqiaġvik on Alaska’s North Slope to collaborate with the local Indigenous Iñupiat community of whalers. She also partnered with Arctic broadband company Quintillion, who provided access to one of their own deep sea telecommunications cables. Amid terabytes of DAS recordings, Bouffaut eventually achieved another first in her field. She became the first person to confirm bowhead whale vocalizations by harnessing fiber-optic cables.

“Being able to detect bowhead whales on a telecommunication cable is the proof of concept we need to show that DAS can be used to monitor all baleen whales,” explained Bouffaut.

It has been revealed that although the newly introduced strategy isn’t sensitive enough to replace dedicated ocean monitoring using underwater microphone arrays, Bouffaut and her colleagues believe DAS could become an invaluable additional tool. It also showcases a way to convert existing infrastructures into multi-use systems.

Industry observers note that “The review is also a call to action for scientists, industry partners and regulators to collaborate,” said Bouffaut. “We now have the technical blueprint to turn global undersea infrastructure into a global network for ocean conservation.”.

Maybe he’d be open to letting someone else take over after that.

Sources indicate that despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Recent findings suggest that despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she stated, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Recent findings suggest that bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

According to recent reports, tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026.
  • Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to upcoming data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a significant catch.

Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to upcoming data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

It has been revealed that sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of newly introduced car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

Sources indicate that UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

In a recent development, even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s newly introduced car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

It has been revealed that chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

It has been revealed that those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

In a recent development, australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Industry observers note that brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

According to recent reports, as the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

#17600. When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1110 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Imagine you and your partner have just finished having dinner with your parents.
  • Eventually, they sigh right before asking, “Why didn’t you say anything when your mother made that comment?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Imagine you and your partner have just finished having dinner with your parents. The drive home seems eerily quiet, even though you feel like the evening went pretty well, and you can’t shake the general impression that your partner is upset.

Eventually, they sigh right before asking, “Why didn’t you say anything when your mother made that comment?”.

It has been revealed that you try to explain that you didn’t want to start an argument. After all, your mother has always been outspoken, and you know from experience that challenging her would have started “a thing” and made everyone uncomfortable. You had assumed your partner understood this and would instinctively know you didn’t agree with what your mother remarked.

Your partner sees things differently. They were embarrassed and went on to spend the entire evening feeling unsupported and increasingly resentful. You’re also beginning to realize that while you might have avoided one argument over the dinner table, you set yourself up to face another one at home.

Situations like these are common for couples managing complicated relationships with extended family. Doing your best to keep everyone happy seems like the responsible adult choice, especially when family gatherings can already be tense or stressful. However, avoiding uncomfortable conversations with relatives can easily come at the expense of your partner.

According to a 2013 longitudinal study, early dynamics with in-laws often correlate with later marital stability. This connection can vary according to factors like race and gender, so complicated family relationships don’t necessarily affect every couple the same way. However, wanting to maintain family harmony is second nature to most people. This can especially be the case for those who grew up in households in which challenging a parent was unacceptable or disagreements almost always escalated into ugly arguments.

It’s easy to go into adulthood with the general idea that keeping quiet is the cleanest way to deal with uncomfortable situations. That doesn’t necessarily stop once you’re in a committed relationship of your own.

Naturally, you love your partner and feel responsible for protecting their feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’re comfortable confronting your parents, siblings, or other relatives.

Picture a situation in which your sibling cracks a joke at your partner’s expense during a family get-together. Everyone laughs, so you join in, even though you also know your partner finds such remarks hurtful.

From your point of view, laughing along was the easiest way to avoid a potential scene, especially if that’s your family’s usual routine when this particular sibling makes off-color comments or gives someone a hard time. Meanwhile, all your partner knows is that you joined in while someone else embarrassed them in front of others.

According to recent reports, disconnects like these can become huge sticking points in a relationship when they happen repeatedly. Your partner may start to associate getting together with your family with having to endure uncomfortable comments and potential embarrassment. If they also feel you expect them to tolerate this, they may eventually wonder whether they can count on you at all when life gets difficult.

Recent findings suggest that A 2019 study published in Social Work Research surveyed 351 women about their relationships with their mothers-in-law. Findings suggested factors like family-triangle dynamics or unclear relationship boundaries directly impacted relationship quality.

Having a partner who stays silent during disagreements can further aggravate relationships that may already be complicated.

When one partner makes a habit of not addressing comments or behaviors that are inappropriate, the other can feel responsible for managing everyone’s discomfort. They’re forced to choose between speaking up and potentially causing a scene or staying silent and dealing with feelings of resentment or abandonment.

Sources indicate that properly supporting your partner doesn’t necessarily mean agreeing with them every time they complain about your family. However, you can (and should) acknowledge your partner’s feelings and talk things out when conflicts come up. There’s a world of difference between saying “You’re right, my family is awful” no matter what and saying “I get why that was hurtful, so let’s talk about it” instead.

Couples can minimize recurring disagreements further by working through expectations before people butt heads and things get tense.

In a recent development, 1. Discuss potential sticking points beforehand. Some relatives may be notorious for disregarding other people’s boundaries or making intrusive comments. If this is the case in your family, prep for upcoming gatherings by talking to your partner beforehand about how you’ll respond to any possible incidents.

Sources indicate that avoid assuming you already know what your partner will find helpful in the moment. Instead, ask them what would truly help them feel supported and go from there.

It has been revealed that 2. Address inappropriate behavior calmly. Intervening if things do get tense doesn’t have to mean starting an argument. Try shutting down hurtful comments, intrusive questions, and so forth by simply saying, “We’d rather not discuss that” or “Please don’t make fun of my partner.”.

Statements like these help establish boundaries with relatives and set expectations without necessarily escalating the situation.

Industry observers note that 3. Avoid volunteering your partner to keep others happy. Instead of instantly making commitments or agreeing to family plans that affect both of you, talk to your partner about it first. Being considerate to your family is notable, but it shouldn’t mean making decisions and promises on someone else’s behalf.

4. Check in privately. If something happens at a family get-together that feels uncomfortable, pull your partner aside and ask how they’re doing. If necessary, talk about it for a moment or offer to leave early. Even a brief check-in is often enough to keep your partner feeling supported and stop resentment from building up through an evening.

According to recent reports, 5. Take responsibility when you get it wrong. You’re only human, so there may be times when you only realize after the fact that staying silent may have hurt your partner. Acknowledge it and explain what happened. Then apologize and express a willingness to respond differently next time.

Conversations like these should go both ways, so be sure to give your partner a chance to explain their own family histories or talk about genuine misunderstandings as well.

Ultimately, it’s more than possible to keep your family relationships strong while also helping your partner feel properly loved and supported. But doing so might mean learning to manage occasional discomfort instead of simply expecting your partner to absorb the impact and understand.

Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting upcoming models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine.
  • Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
  • Recent findings suggest that we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the firm announced aims to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting upcoming models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

Recent findings suggest that we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the firm announced aims to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

Industry observers note that but don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a organization with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

Industry observers note that the UC3 originally introduced in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t unveiled any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

Recent findings suggest that in much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

In a recent development, I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost concern - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

#17598. Tech Report: Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

Tech Report: Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (385 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that about 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture.
  • The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE.
  • “This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that about 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations highlights that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

Industry observers note that “Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, remarked in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”.

Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, upcoming research suggests.
  • In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.
  • They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million upcoming cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, upcoming research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million upcoming cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 latest cases a year, the researchers estimated.

In a recent development, about 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

It has been revealed that the researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she remarked.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang noted those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang said that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang noted she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The Newly introduced England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Recent findings suggest that the AHA stated potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen remarked.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

According to recent reports, huang noted that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang stated she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 newly introduced EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of upcoming public EV charging stations.

In a recent development, “The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

It has been revealed that the rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, upcoming data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

#17592. Before You Blueprint Thanksgiving Dinner, Plan Family Dynamics

Before You Blueprint Thanksgiving Dinner, Plan Family Dynamics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • In a recent development, by this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving.
  • According to recent reports, will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

In a recent development, by this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving. We’re discussing who’s coming, who’s bringing what, and whether people prefer the canned or fresh cranberry sauce. We may also be planning conversations that haven’t happened.

According to recent reports, will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet? Will our parenting become a topic of discussion? Will we spend another holiday doing the work while everyone else watches football?

I have written about the friction that can accompany family gatherings. As Thanksgiving approaches again, I keep wondering would it would look like to prepare for the family dynamics as thoughtfully as we prepare for the meal.

Think about the moment you’re most concerned about. Perhaps it’s a particular question, a familiar disagreement, or the expectation that you’ll organize everything. Now consider what you’re predicting. Are you anticipating a situation that happens regularly? Or are you imagining several possible arguments and preparing a response to each one? Past experiences give us useful information, but mentally replaying an argument doesn’t necessarily give us a useful plan.

Try making the concern specific: “I’m worried someone will comment on my career decision.” Then identify a response you would feel comfortable using: “I’m comfortable with my decision, and I’m not looking for advice about it today.” You may still feel uncomfortable and dread having the conversation but having a response ready simply gives you somewhere to begin.

Industry observers note that we often approach holidays with goals that depend on other people, like everyone will get along, no one will make an insensitive comment, or everyone will appreciate the effort. Those hopes are understandable, but they’re also difficult to guarantee.

In a recent development, consider a few decisions you can make yourself. How long will you stay? Which preparations can you reasonably take on? What will you do if a conversation becomes uncomfortable? You might decide to visit for dessert rather than spend the entire day. You might ask someone else to bring the side dishes. You might arrange transportation so you can leave when you’re ready.

These decisions deserve space alongside the grocery list.

If a familiar pattern bothers you, consider whether there’s a request you can make before the gathering. For example, if you usually manage the meal and cleanup, “I need more help this year” is a starting point. A more specific request gives others a clearer way to participate: “Can you handle the dishes after dinner, including putting the leftovers away?”.

Sources indicate that the same applies to traditions. If the usual schedule no longer works for your household, raise that glitch while looks are being made. Others may be disappointed. You can acknowledge that disappointment while still explaining what you can offer.

In an uncomfortable moment, finding the right words can be difficult. Choose language that sounds like something you would actually say. For an intrusive question: “I don’t have anything I want to share about that.” For unsolicited advice: “I’ll ask if I need suggestions.” For a conversation you want to leave: “I’m going to step away for a few minutes.”.

A prepared phrase won’t determine how another person responds. It can help you communicate your own decision more clearly.

Industry observers note that preparation can also include thinking about what you’re looking forward to: Is there someone you’d like to spend time with? A recipe you want to learn? A game, walk, or family story you’d enjoy sharing? Make a little room for that experience rather than assuming it will happen once everything else is finished.

According to recent reports, once you’re home after the gathering, give yourself a fair assessment of the day. One awkward exchange doesn’t have to define the entire gathering. You can appreciate the parts you enjoyed and think honestly about what you’d change next time.

Thanksgiving takes preparation. Along with deciding what belongs on the table, we can decide what we have the time, energy, and willingness to bring to it.
