#17590. Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1241 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • According to recent reports, OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared reveals a latest-generation Model Y in traffic.

The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

According to recent reports, OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Recent findings suggest that careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

In a recent development, this isn’t latest in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

Industry observers note that the U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Sources indicate that now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

Recent findings suggest that since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual indicates about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

According to recent reports, in other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

The penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

Sources indicate that and Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk mentioned in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

Recent findings suggest that the Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

Recent findings suggest that we’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

Recent findings suggest that people have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

In a recent development, but police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

The fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#17589. Driven: Porsche 911 Challenge Is a More Accessible Race Car

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1140 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Roadandtrack ↗ Open Full Page

Driven: Porsche 911 Challenge Is a More Accessible Race Car

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Next year will mark the 40th running of the Porsche Mobil 1 Supercup, the one-make race series so ubiquitous you hardly need either Porsche or 911 qualifiers for somebody to know what you mean by “Cup car.” Like other sports cars with long histories, the further you go back in time, the more similar the racing 911 is to the roadgoing version.
  • Early 964 Cup cars are, like Ferrari’s 355 Challenge, road legal with normal VIN codes.
  • Recent findings suggest that I tried the 992 Cup Car.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Next year will mark the 40th running of the Porsche Mobil 1 Supercup, the one-make race series so ubiquitous you hardly need either Porsche or 911 qualifiers for somebody to know what you mean by “Cup car.” Like other sports cars with long histories, the further you go back in time, the more similar the racing 911 is to the roadgoing version. Likewise, the further forward you move, the more they diverge.

Early 964 Cup cars are, like Ferrari’s 355 Challenge, road legal with normal VIN codes. They were stripped, caged versions of standard Carreras. I’m leaving out a lot of hardworking engineers’ tweaks here, but the point is that there was a time that driving a Cup car felt mostly like a normal car with more noise, fewer comforts, and better safety equipment. The 1999 996-generation Cup still used a coded key and had a normal clutch and an H-pattern 6-speed—it was just a very sticky GT3. But the 997 generation of 2005 was the fork in the road, introducing a sequential gearbox. The 2013 991-gen brought in a motorsport engine-management system and electronics. And the 992 generation that races today nominally resembles a 911 but operates nothing like one and requires a team to run it.

Recent findings suggest that I tried the 992 Cup Car. It is incredibly intimidating. I do not have what it takes to be successful in a car like that, and I would not want to have to round up a posse to go for a drive, even if the performance is staggering. Instead what I really want, as do many other amateur and wannabe racers, is a race car that closely resembles their road car. Hence the popularity of the GT3 RS. If the car never leaves the track property, why get a GT3 RS when you could get an Oreca LMP for $100k less? Because it’s not really about being street legal; it’s about being approachable and turnkey.

The car for regular weekend warriors used to be the GT4/RS Clubsport, but sadly, the 718-generation Cayman is now dead and buried. Earlier this year, rumors swirled that Porsche was prepping a 911 GT4 to take the Cayman’s place, and the story ran alongside photos of a racy-looking camouflaged 992 GT3. It turns out that Porsche is going GT4 racing with the 911, but that will be a modified Cup car, not the one from those pictures. Instead, the images were of the car you see here, the latest 911 Challenge. Essentially, it’s the old GT3 Cup car concept for today’s country-club weekend warriors: an upfitted, stripped, and caged GT3 road car.

According to recent reports, A roll cage can only make a car so approachable, but once I’d stopped and crawled into the comfy seat, things got familiar quickly, as I was looking at the complete 992-generation dashboard, gauge cluster, and center console. The steering wheel is straight out of the GT3 RS (though without an airbag installed). After strapping in with the multipoint harnesses,I pressed the original start button on the left, and the 4.0-liter flat-six fired just like a standard GT3. The Challenge retains the factory heating and ventilation; the road car’s touchscreen display is gone, replaced by a blank panel with emergency cutoff and fire switches.

According to recent reports, mechanically, it’s barely changed from the GT3. The engine makes six more horsepower, now 508 hp total, thanks to a race-specific exhaust setup. But it still uses the standard, seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission, so you can just put it in drive if you prefer, or shift using the paddles.

My drive in the Challenge was brief. Just four laps around the 2.5-mile Circuit Ricardo Tormo, following on from my four-car Manthey test. For context, with factory race driver Timo Bernhard driving this circuit, the Challenge almost perfectly splits the range: 4.6 seconds per lap slower than a Cup, and 5.2 seconds quicker than a GT3 Weissach. Notably, it’s also 1.6 seconds quicker per lap than the GT3 RS Manthey. Where it gets interesting is in the details.

A GT3 RS Manthey is on road-legal tires but with enormous downforce. The Challenge is on slicks but with the same aero package as a standard GT3.

So if you’re willing to throw away street legality, for $275,000 (less than the cost of many standard GT3s) you can go far quicker on a track than you could with the fastest road-legal 911 you can buy, the Manthey GT3 RS, which would knock on the door of half a million dollars.

Everything about the Challenge is easy. As long as you’re reasonably comfortable on a slick tire, the rest of the car comes directly to you. The Challenge is far more reliant on mechanical grip than downforce, so you can start learning the car by going much quicker through hairpins than you ever have before, rather than having to learn it by going full send over a blind crest in sixth gear, with potentially scary consequences.

It has been revealed that likewise, because there isn’t 2200 pounds of downforce, the Challenge isn’t sprung too stiffly, so you don’t take abuse on bumpy curbing. The knobs for traction control and PTV work essentially the same as the GT3 RS, just with new programming specific to the Challenge.

Sources indicate that I’m not going to pretend, in five laps, to have a thorough understanding of the dynamics of the 911 Challenge, or to say that I took it to its limit. I had just enough time to get comfortable, which is more than I can say about other race cars.

What I did have was an incredible time on the track. The Challenge is the kind of car that inspired me to want to push it harder, but the “race car” bits of it disappeared into the background, so I could focus on things happening outside rather than things inside. It was instantly comfortable and familiar, and a place I could spend all day. Three-hour double stint in an enduro? That would be no problem. Also, possible thanks to the 29-gallon fuel cell.

Industry observers note that there will be a one-make series for the 911 Challenge, and initially Porsche wants to sell them to folks who intend to enter, but that’s not really the point—this is the 911 race car that most 911 owners actually want. It is a fun, flexible, approachable, and fizzy experience that elevates what they already love about the 911 and can race if they want to, but that won’t require a whole team if they just want to rip off a few laps after work. And for less money than the road car, not more.

It’s the race car for people who want their race car to feel like a 911, not like a corporation.

A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (535 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile.
  • Sources indicate that astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

Recent findings suggest that “We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”.

Sources indicate that astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies upcoming planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” noted Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so swiftly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”.

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

In a recent development, yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.

Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.
  • The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.
  • Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, stated in a news release.

Sources indicate that “For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can rapidly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s vital for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

“Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula mentioned.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but stated the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”.

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”.

It has been revealed that cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

It has been revealed that “Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”.

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he remarked that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”.

Recent findings suggest that an AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

“Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”.

According to recent reports, other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen stated.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”.

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen remarked.

“Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”.

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

It has been revealed that researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

According to recent reports, other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen stated.

“Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”.

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:.

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he mentioned.

In a recent development, still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:.

According to recent reports, “I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”.

#17585. How to Become Change-Curious

How to Become Change-Curious

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station).
  • What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station). Messages about change are inescapable and part of the background noise of everyday life. Often we ignore the onslaught of “be better, do better” messaging, and other times we eagerly try to change ourselves because we so passionately want our lives to be different.

What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?

Industry observers note that like any troubling relationship, it can be useful to explore some of the dynamics that are not working for us. If we are fortunate to find ourselves changing with ease and little friction, that is a cause to celebrate. For most of us, at least some of the time, we have some difficult experiences engaging in change. We might tell ourselves that change is good; that we should want it. Such a message is difficult to accept when we are not certain change is what we want or need. We might also believe that if we don’t want change, there must be something wrong with us; we are resistant or self-sabotaging or anxious or overwhelmed. Some of these things might be true, but labeling ourselves brings up shame, and shame can be crippling, as it can bring to mind past failures or negative messaging.

Sources indicate that change can also be hard because it takes work. Even if we are completely inspired and motivated to change, developing habits and learning newly introduced ways to do things takes time; a recent study found it takes an average of 66 days for a habit to form. For any individual, it can take more or less time for a behavior change to become automatic.

Industry observers note that change is work; it takes time and disrupts our lives. We have cognitive, emotional, and behavioral friction that makes it more difficult to start and complete. Yet, despite the difficulty, we seek change. We want our lives to improve, so we purchase lots of self-help, coaching, therapy, gym memberships, food plans, and surgeries to get started. Across cultures throughout the lifespan, some aspects of change and growth are constantly occurring as we seek to change ourselves and our circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that given that change is both hard and something we desire, what if we considered approaching the change process with a learner’s mind? Instead of forcing ourselves to endure change or shaming ourselves into it, we can befriend change through cultivating curiosity about all it has to offer. Wondering about change and being open to all the ways we show up in the change process has the potential to make change less daunting.

We have many options to be curious about change.

According to recent reports, noticing change in our environment, and then noticing change in ourselves. We can start by spending some time noticing change in the weather or change in plants. Maybe we notice how construction or demolition is changing a neighborhood, or how our neighbor's families are changing and growing. We can then consider changes in our own experience over the years—in our living situations, job, or social life. We can notice the ones that have been the most meaningful. How did these changes happen? Some changes occur because of luck or circumstances, and it is likely that we were able to take advantage of our good fortune. Some changes occur because we worked hard at making change. How did we do it? What characteristics helped us become a “changer,” and how could we tap into those characteristics if we wanted to change again?

Envisioning what change might look like. This is a common approach to increasing motivation for change. What if we decided we could envision something for ourselves in the same way we read a book or watch a movie? We could envision being in a few different situations and view our story with wonder instead of expectation.

In a recent development, looking at the process more than the outcome. We tend to be outcome-oriented. We see products that promise to help us build muscle, learn a language, or see younger, more beautiful skin in a few weeks or a couple of months. The promise of relatively quick fixes is so compelling that even when we logically understand there is no way a product can live up to our expectations, we might find ourselves literally buying it. Purchasing a service or product to help us change is not necessarily a problem, and it can be a good thing. Expecting the product to have specific outcomes is where we can become discouraged. So many things impact the actual outcome of our attempts to change: time, environment, our body limits and composition, other demands taking our time.

Shifting our attention to the process requires that we step away from holding the outcome as our top priority. Instead, it’s about going along for the ride and adopting a perspective that we are learning and improving our lives by noticing how we feel after engaging in exercise, making the effort to practice a latest instrument, or consuming nutritious foods.

Sampling change. We can check it out and see what it does for us. Events such as Sober October or Dry January were created to help drinkers wanting to explore, but not commit to, changing their drinking behaviors—to test out life without (or with less) alcohol. Virtually any change can be tested out and explored. Sampling a fresh behavior is not the same as engaging in a dedicated lifestyle change, but it allows for some action. It also provides an opportunity to approach a new way of being in a manner that reduces overwhelm; a chance to wonder about what might be possible.

Curiosity is a powerful frame of mind. It has the potential to tame the intensity of change and open up possibilities for transformation that come from the power of exploration and wonder.

Shigeoka, S. (2024, June 6). How deep curiosity can change the world [Interview by T. Burnett]. John Templeton Foundation. https://www.templeton.org/news/how-deep-curiosity-can-change-the-world.

Recent findings suggest that want to play with dogs at the airport and have it be for a good cause? Well, boy, do we have the volunteer gig for you. It’s actually less playtime and more very serious Transportation Security Administration (TSA) work, but there’s still dogs, so we consider that a win: The TSA is currently looking for volunteers to be explosive detection K9 decoys, and honestly there may not be a cuter way to spend a weekend. Let these very smart dogs show us all just how smart they really are!

In their call for volunteers, the TSA claims that a volunteer shift with these crafty canines “may feel like a high-stakes game of hide and seek.” They also emphasize that “this training is a serious and important part of keeping our canine teams ready for duty.”.

Sources indicate that you’re basically pretending to be an airport bad guy or, as the TSA puts it, “a covert role player.” You might be tasked with carrying a “training item” and wander around an airport acting like you’re just an everyday passenger in the ticketing lobbies, going through security, or just generally waiting around for their boarding time. Then, the real game begins, and the canine team will try to sniff you out.

The entire set-up is meant to mimic what these dogs might face in the real world.

The entire volunteer shift takes about two to three hours.

There aren’t a ton of restrictions on who can volunteer with these very smart doggies. You have to be at least 18 years old to volunteer. Although minors can volunteer alongside an adult companion, they can only participate in limited ways.

You also have to be comfortable sitting, walking, and moving around an airport. However, wheelchair and scooter users can participate in the program.

You can check out their annual calendar, which will be available in November or December. A German shorthaired pointer named Bolt won the TSA’S Cutest Canine Contest for 2026 and will be one of the working dogs featured on the 2027 calendar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, overlanding doesn’t exactly come with a fixed set of rules. As long as the vehicle makes it off the trail at the end of the journey, whether it’s after an hour or a year, the mission has been accomplished—and Ford’s latest Expedition build is designed to stay out and make the most of the great outdoors in a way real overlanders can get behind.

Recent findings suggest that the latest rig, officially known as the Project Overland Expedition Tremor, pushes Dearborn’s full-size SUV to its off-road limit. Ford partnered with Fox Factory Vehicles on it, and added Raptor-inspired running boards, modified skid plates, and suspension tweaks that deliver up to 10.6 inches of ground clearance to the three-row SUV. The package also includes F-150 Raptor R wheels, BFGoodrich All-Terrain T/A KO2 tires, a two-inch lift kit with FOX 2.0 Performance Series Coilovers, and a modular F-150 Tremor front bumper.

According to recent reports, dependability and recovery are key on an overlander, and Ford didn’t skimp in this regard. A Ford Raptor hidden front winch mount and a WARN winch comes fitted to the three-row SUV. To keep its twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 running cool behind that winch, Ford also upgraded the Expedition’s intercooler.

Recent findings suggest that the Project Overland Expedition Tremor also includes Rigid Phoenix ditch and roof lights, DC scene lights, and a set of Tred Pro recovery boards with quick-release mounting pins. Ford wired all of these lighting accessories into a central overhead panel, allowing for easy action while on-trail. Of course, camping on top of your vehicle is all but required while overlanding, so Ford added a Yakima SkyRise HD softshell rooftop tent, liftgate side curtains, OverNOut awning, LockNLoad platform, and TimberLine Towers.

Ford Project Overland Expedition Tremor.

According to recent reports, “We chose every component on purpose. Each one helps you travel farther, stay longer, and explore more confidently. Project Overland is more than a single build. It's a test bed,” Michael Kress, senior manager of advanced design & engineering for Fox Factory Performance Vehicle Development, remarked. “Ford and Fox Factory Vehicles have been learning what customers want from a purpose-built full-size overlanding SUV and exploring where we might collaborate next.”.

It has been revealed that the phrase “test bed” may be a tease, but it’s also a bit promising. Ford has not confirmed that more extreme off-roaders are coming, but the OEM-like quality of this build certainly shows that the automaker is capable of it. Sadly, Ford specified that this project vehicle would not be sold to the public, but we’d sure like to take this special Expedition Tremor deep into the woods.

A Upcoming York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#17581. Can one intense workout per week keep you healthy? Here’s the science.

Can one intense workout per week keep you healthy? Here’s the science.

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the so-called “weekend warrior” exercise approach offers an enticing trade: skip the workouts all week, and cram them into one or two days instead.
  • Still, for people who genuinely lack the time to exercise during the workweek, this approach could offer real convenience—and real health benefits.
  • A recent study in Hong Kong has supported that idea, finding that people who packed all their weekly exercise into one high-intensity interval training (HIIT) session lost about as much body fat as those who spread the same workout across three sessions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the so-called “weekend warrior” exercise approach offers an enticing trade: skip the workouts all week, and cram them into one or two days instead. It sounded great to me, until I realized it could turn my hard-earned “Thank God it’s Friday” into “Oh God, it’s Friday.”.

Still, for people who genuinely lack the time to exercise during the workweek, this approach could offer real convenience—and real health benefits.

A recent study in Hong Kong has supported that idea, finding that people who packed all their weekly exercise into one high-intensity interval training (HIIT) session lost about as much body fat as those who spread the same workout across three sessions.

In a recent development, so, is doing all your exercise in one session really just as good as spreading it out? The answer depends on your goals and overall health. But according to Dr. Keith Diaz, an exercise physiologist at Columbia University, even infrequent exercise has real value.

Recent findings suggest that “You don’t have to be a daily gym goer to reap the benefits,” he says. “Some exercise, even if it’s just one time a week, provides health benefits.”.

The study, published in Nature Communications, spent 16 weeks following 315 adults who were overweight or had central obesity. The researchers split the participants into three groups, with one doing a single 75-minute HIIT session per week, and another spreading this exercise across three weekly sessions.

“They had participants do three 25-minute HIIT sessions of 4 minutes hard and 3 minutes easy,” Diaz states. “There was 15 to 30 minutes between HIIT sessions, plus a 5-minute warm-up and 5-minute cool-down.” The once-weekly group did all three of those 25-minute blocks in a single visit; the second group spread them into three visits across the week, one block per visit. A third group, the controls, did not exercise, and instead attended health education classes.

Sources indicate that by the end of the 16 weeks, both HIIT groups had lost more body fat than the control group. Specifically, the once-weekly group lost about 1.75 pounds more than the control group, and the group that exercised three times a week lost 2.2 pounds more. Waist circumference, which is a measure of central obesity, also improved significantly in both exercise groups compared to control.

In a recent development, “These were relatively modest reductions in fat,” Diaz says. Neither group reported any exercise-related injuries.

The researchers measured much more than fat loss. They also tracked cardiorespiratory fitness, which is a measure of how efficiently the body uses oxygen during exercise, and a strong predictor of long-term health.

By this measure, the two workout groups did not perform equally. The group that exercised three times a week achieved roughly an 11 percent improvement in cardiorespiratory fitness, compared with an approximate 6 percent improvement in the once-weekly group. Diaz has a theory for why this might be the case.

“Physiologically, the more frequently you stress your body with exercise, the more it will adapt and yield changes to your heart, blood vessels, and muscles,” he says.

Sources indicate that so, if fat loss is your main priority, a “weekend warrior” workout might be enough. However, Diaz believes the study actually makes a case for spreading exercise across the week “if your focus is on being fitter and generally being more healthy.”.

Recent findings suggest that so who does stand to benefit from squeezing a week’s worth of exercise into one session? According to Diaz, the ideal “weekend warrior” is a healthy person who, because of the demands of their daily lives, might not get around to exercising otherwise.

“This approach is best suited for generally healthy individuals who are short on time during the week and struggle to exercise because of their busy weekday schedule,” he states.

Recent findings suggest that however, some people with preexisting health conditions might not see the most benefit from this highly consolidated regimen. In particular, Diaz claims people with diabetes or hypertension should try to be physically active every day.

“Exercise lowers blood sugar and blood pressure for 12 to 24 hours afterward,” he says. “So, the weekend warrior approach would not be ideally suitable for individuals with diabetes or hypertension, who need these regular reductions in blood sugar or blood pressure.” Diaz adds that people with heart conditions should discuss once-weekly HIIT with their doctors before starting.

You might be eating too much protein.

Do rage workouts really help to blow off steam?

Are ‘hot’ workout classes better?

You should start taking ‘Fart Walks’.

Should you work out on an empty stomach? Fitness experts weigh in.

How much exercise do I need to stay healthy?

No, you don’t need 10,000 steps a day.

Although the once-weekly approach has undeniable appeal and might truly benefit some busy folks, Diaz notes that it’s not exactly the magical quick fix some headlines would suggest.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the headlines around one day of exercise a week melting belly fat are misleading,” he says. “Yes, it’s one day of exercise, but it’s a lot in one day.”.

In a recent development, although the exercise itself takes 75 minutes in total, adding time to warm up and rest between the sessions means that the single weekly workout takes almost three hours to complete. And it’s not melting the fat away.

Despite that deflating reality check, Diaz sees real potential in this approach when healthy people use it appropriately.

It has been revealed that “This study adds further support that some exercise, even if just on the weekend, is better than none,” he states. “So if the weekend is the only time you have to exercise, this could be an option for you.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that THE BEST HIKING season is in full swing (fall, and we’ll die on that hill). And winter hiking isn’t that far ahead. So, it’s high time to get your go-to trail gear dialed in. Check your backpack for rips, reseal your tent seams, and make sure there’s enough tread on your favorite hiking boots (or shoes).

In a recent development, if anything needs replacing or upgrading, we’ve put together a guide to the best hiking gear, according to continual testing by our team of outdoor editors and experts. From UPF clothing and waterproof shoes to camp stoves and portable power packs, here’s everything we always pack when hitting the trail, whether for a day hike or even looking to be out there for a few days. And for cooler treks, there’s always some cold weather hiking gear made specific for the task.

As an outdoors writer, I’ve spent countless weeks outside each year for decades. During that time, I've put the most popular hiking gear to the test in places like Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of Upcoming Hampshire, the vast deserts of Massive Bend National Park, Antarctica, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on his top picks, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, usefulness, weight, durability, materials, functionality, and more.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or need the perfect stove for a full-fledged expedition, we've got you covered with the best hiking gear.

Recent findings suggest that the latest version of the Adidas Terrex Freehiker blends understated street-friendly style with serious trail-ready chops. The low-key aesthetic (especially in core black) plays well with just about any casual outfit, making it a great travel-friendly shoe when you want to pack just one. But, with a Continental rubber outsole and liberal use of Gore-Tex, it’s ready for whatever off-pavement adventures you’re cooking up.

Osprey’s Kestrel 45 is the perfect “all things for all hikers” pack, especially for those looking to buy just one bag. The 45-liter capacity is well-sized for day hikes and overnighters. It features a classic rucksack silhouette, but with all the best features of a modern pack, including comfortable straps and a hip belt, plus a well-ventilated back panel. Storage (pockets, loops, and lash points) is well thought out, and it’s hydration reservoir compatible to boot.

Read More: Best Hiking Backpacks.

Mammut’s deceptively simple Runbold IV hiking pants are among the best we’ve ever worn. The lightweight, four-way stretch fabric and adjustable waistband are crazy comfortable and allow you to move freely on the trail. Four zippered pockets offer just enough storage for your essentials, and all keep everything close to the body thanks to a more streamlined, athletic fit than most.

It’s not quite a hiking boot, a hiking shoe, or a trail runner—it’s somehow neither and all three in one. The lightweight construction and stiff upper support fast-moving day hikes over challenging terrain. A rock-solid blend of technical materials—namely Gore-Tex Invisible Fit, Vibram Megagrip, and ballistic mesh—makes for our favorite hiking footwear of the year. It’s durable, comfortable, sticks to anything, and is completely waterproof too.

At a minimum, a smartphone and satellite messenger are required packing for most hikers these days, so it’s always good to carry backup power for both. Nestout’s 10000mAh Power Bank is compact, relatively lightweight, and waterproof, making this middle-of-the-pack model the perfect solution for most hikers. Every model in the lineup provides USB-C and/or USB-A ports for keeping your most essential gadgets humming in the backcountry.

In a recent development, hardcore hikers could argue the virtues of Merino versus synthetic until the sun goes supernova. For us, a blended construction of both is best. Smartwool’s new Active Mesh Short Sleeve T takes a mostly Merino wool design and adds just the right amount of Lyocell and polyester. The result is a near-perfect hiking shirt that’s lightweight, breathable, quick wicking, and odor-resistant.

Sources indicate that we’ll take a collapsible water bottle over a traditional Nalgene any day of the week. This 1-liter model is lightweight, inexpensive, and collapses down very small when empty. Plus, the capacity and built-in filter make this a no-brainer for using as your main water bottle or as a backup. With even a remotely drinkable water source along your route, you’re guaranteed clean, potable hydration almost indefinitely.

The right insect repellent is key for spraying on both yourself and your gear. For the latter, we treat all of our outerwear (plus boots and socks) with this purpose-built solution from Sawyer. The permethrin-based product is safe for most fabrics and creates a durable, effective layer of skin-safe protection that fends off ticks, mosquitoes, and other bitey bugs while lasting over a month, even when machine-washed.

Recent findings suggest that UPF hoodies suffer from a sea of sameness. That’s why the Path Projects Wadi 2.0 stands out: It feels and performs differently. The difference being the Toray Fieldsensor Byokan fabric that Path Projects uses. It’s a lightweight material that’s just as durable while also wicking moisture incredibly well. A snap on the hood provides even better neck coverage (and keeps the hood on when moving quickly), and welded sleeve cuffs help your sleeves go over your hands or be pushed up.

True to its namesake, Darn Tough’s socks offer bulletproof durability that I haven’t found in any other sock brand. Their Hike Micro Crew is my go-to for every hike with seamless toe construction and a just-right stretch and cushioning that’s just as comfortable at mile 10 or 100. It’s designed with a “performance fit” that stays put without slipping or bunching, which translates to blissful blister-free hiking. It’s pricey compared to other brands, but I’ve had several pairs for years and they still look good as new. Plus, DT backs all of their products with an unconditional lifetime guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that even for hikers not regularly trekking out after dark, packing a headlamp just in case is wise. This basic model from Black Diamond is simple, easy to use, and budget-friendly. The compact, low-profile design practically disappears in any backpack, and it can run off of two different types of battery (either standard AAAs or BD’s own rechargeable 1500 lithium-ion cell).

Nothing beats a zip-up fleece hoodie as an extra layer for maximum “toss in the backpack” versatility, and Marmot’s PrimaLoft Evolve Aerothermal Hoody has been my go-to for months now. The inside is as soft as a teddy bear, while the 100 percent recycled ripstop polyester shell helps block some wind and light rain. As the name implies, it’s bolstered with a good dose of PrimaLoft Evolve, making it ideal as an insulating layer in cold weather and a standalone outer layer the rest of the year. At just 10 ounces, it’s incredibly lightweight and packs down small, too, meaning it’s perfect as a “just in case” layer.

According to recent reports, your smartphone might be the most expensive piece of gear in your hiking loadout, so why not protect it on the trail? OtterBox’s Sole Series Pack provides rugged protection via a rubberized shell and raised edges to shield your screen—all with a dash of modern style. A clever elastic rope on the back offers extra storage space for small essentials like lip balm or your driver’s license.

In a recent development, you can’t rely on your smartphone in the backcountry. For couples or groups hiking together, dedicated off-grid-ready communication is essential. Rocky Talkie’s Mountain Radio is ridiculously small and clips to a backpack so it stays out of the way until you need it. It’s great for regular check-ins or keeping in contact if you’re ever separated from the group, especially in cell service dead zones. Plus, the four-day battery life is ideal for longer treks.

Industry observers note that trekking poles are a godsend over difficult terrain. For those times when you need to prioritize featherweight, travel-friendly design over hardcore durability and heavy-duty usability, Helinox’s Passport TL115 are superb. They collapse to a pack-friendly 14 inches when not in use, but adjust to accommodate a wide variety of hikers once unfurled to their max length of 45.5 inches. With EVA foam grips, DAC aluminum alloy shafts, and a lightweight design (just 11.5 ounces for the pair), these are the perfect balance for most hikers’ needs.

Read More: Do I Need to Use Trekking Poles?

According to recent reports, when even a daypack is a little too much, a sling is just the trick. REI’s Trailmade Hydration Sling is purpose-built for carrying just enough water and your smallest essentials for a few hours on the trail. I love that it includes a HydraPak water bottle (which makes the already reasonable price feel like a steal), but is also hydration reservoir compatible. The interior is roomy enough for up to 4.5 liters’ worth of gear (think car keys, bug spray, trail maps, and the like), and a stretchy pocket on the padded shoulder strap is the perfect place to stash your smartphone.

Sources indicate that packing a camp chair for a day hike or even longer backcountry excursions might seem an unnecessary luxury. But don’t knock it till you’ve tried it. Crazy Creek’s ultra-portable Hex 2.0 folds and rolls for easy transport, but sets up in seconds at camp or vistas to provide the perfect place to pseudo-lounge after a long day on the trail.

It has been revealed that the new PreCip Evo Pro is something of a unicorn in waterproof shells. It’s lightweight, packable, and 100 percent seam-taped for maximum waterproofing—heavier duty than most featherweight “just in case” rain jackets, but lighter and more packable than the sort of hardcore shell you’d pack for a week in the PNW backcountry. Translation: It’s the perfect level of protection against rain for most hikers. Plus, it’s reasonably priced to boot.

It has been revealed that peak Design’s entire line of cleverly designed backpacks is endlessly versatile. The entry-level 18-liter version of the brand’s fan-favorite Outdoor Backpack is perfectly suited for fast-moving, light-packing summit assaults and quick day hikes. The design transitions seamlessly from the office (or airport or train station) to the trail with a rugged-enough construction and streamlined aesthetic that provides everything you need and nothing you don’t in a hybrid daypack.

It has been revealed that first and foremost, you might not need any gear other than hiking shoes (or boots) and the clothes on your back. Hiking can be as simple as a 20-minute walk on a path to a multiweek expedition through the wilderness. Hiking more than 30 minutes? You probably want to figure out some sort of hydration at the least. The shorter the hike, the less gear (in theory) you should be toting with you.

According to recent reports, depending on how deep in the wilderness you’re going (or not going) will determine what sort of gear you might need. Even if it’s only a hike for a few hours, if you’re going into wilderness it takes a different mindset for preparedness (and gear) than it does walking on a dirt path in a park in town. The more remote your hike, the more gear you will probably end up needing.

Weather is a major factor when going on a hike. In cooler climates (or when going up in altitude) you’ll need to factor in layers for warmth. In warmer climates, water will be even more key and lighter layers that can shed moisture and protect you from the sun are key. The conditions of the trail (wet, muddy, rocky, dry, etc.) also determine your footwear choice.

Recent findings suggest that the great thing about hiking is you don’t need any experience to start. The most veteran hikers can share the same trails with first-timers, and everyone in between. But knowing what you’re capable of and comfortable with is crucial. Hiking with a friend is always recommended, but if hiking solo, make sure you inform someone of your location and timing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that some things are meant for showing off: engagement rings, watches, fancy manicures, face tattoos. If nobody notices, what was the point of spending all that money? Other purchases are more subtle, like a well-cut jacket or a youthful neck. They make you look rich, but nobody can quite pinpoint why. The 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S680 is the first kind. There’s no modesty to the Maybach, but as a symbol of prosperity, it won’t be ignored.

Maybach models are for buyers who think the S-class is nice but could make do with more. More bespoke badging, more unique colorways—and more cylinders, at least for lucky shoppers in Asia, the Middle East, and here in the United States. We get the option of a twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V-12, a gem rarer than a diamond in these mini-mill times. Maybach also offers the S580 with a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8, which is far more sensible, quicker, and more fuel efficient . . . but nobody should shop a Maybach with any of those descriptors in mind.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94301.

Recent findings suggest that the Maybach is nearly 18 feet of two-tone paint and illuminated callouts. The front grille is a waterfall of chrome flanked by lacy insets of repeated Maybach logos. The LED headlights are three-pointed stars surrounded by rose gold. Even the Maybach badges on the C-pillars glow to ensure that at no time, day or night, will anyone fail to notice what you’re driving.

And people do notice. At a gas station stop, a man in a Honda called over from the opposite pump, “Hey, that’s some hard work right there.” If I had purchased the car myself, I would have felt proud to have my effort recognized. As it was, I admitted to stolen valor, but I still drove off floating on air. That wasn’t from the compliment, though; the Maybach uses a upcoming air-spring suspension that can anticipate bumps and potholes using cloud-based data from other Mercedes cars on the same road for real-time predictive damping.

Sources indicate that with its long, 133.7-inch wheelbase and outrageously kitted-out back seat (we’ll get to that), it’s obvious that the S680 was designed with rear passengers in mind, but it’s so fun to drive that I’m tempted to take up a chauffeur job. The V-12 is as smooth as a beurre blanc and as meaty as the filet beneath it. It doesn’t move out with the instant response of a V-8 or an electric setup, but such haste is unseemly. Instead, it steps out with authority and builds up steam like a locomotive pulling a private railcar. The only stumble it makes is when the stop-start system kicks the V-12 back into action. Unlike with the V-8’s 48-volt assist, a noticeable shudder accompanies the return of the 12-pot’s combustion. Thankfully, it’s a problem easily solved by deactivating the system with a single push of a button. It’s not like you’re getting good fuel economy with this monster anyway.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94301.

It has been revealed that the S680 is a thirsty machine, with an EPA combined fuel-economy estimate of 14 mpg. Our test car was a mossy silver and white two-tone with a sage leather interior, and that’s the only thing green about it. At least you’ll get lots of compliments at every single gas station.

Industry observers note that the steering and its optional rear-axle assist makes the long car turn in a relatively small circle, and the brakes (15.4-inch ventilated and cross-drilled rotors in the front, 14.2-inch ventilated units in the back) do a heroic job of stopping all 5336 pounds. At the test track—where technical editor Dan Edmunds would not let me ride in the back during testing despite my assertion that it would be more accurate to the car’s use case—the Maybach accelerated to 60 mph in 4.5 seconds. At the world’s fanciest drag strip, it would cross the quarter-mile mark in 12.6 seconds at 118 mph. Edmunds brought it back down to zero from 70 mph in 177 feet without a hint of brake fade. Most impressive, the S680 whipped up 0.90 g of grip around the skidpad. Not bad for something my neighbor Shirley described as “bigger and nicer than my whole house.”.

The Maybach is not actually bigger than Shirley’s house, but she doesn’t have a leather-covered massaging recliner. The S680 has four. Our test car was equipped with the $6000 Executive Rear Seat Package Plus, among many other extras, and be forewarned that if you invite neighbors, gym buddies, or your hair stylist to check out the leather-covered footrests, Maybach-branded pillows, yacht-striped wooden console, folding lunch trays, and back-seat wine cooler with champagne-flute-specific cup holders, they might be unwilling to vacate the premises. I thought I might have to give the car back with a full crew inside.

According to recent reports, the Maybach is excessive. It’s not about providing a quiet space or restrained elegance. Every surface that isn’t covered in leather or wood is an interactive screen. The Maybach gets Benz’s theater-wide Superscreen with a 12.3-inch driver display that merges with a 14.4-inch center screen and a 12.3-inch passenger display. Everything glows, or is gold, or is both golden and glowing. In some of Mercedes’s other cars, the Superscreen feels tacky, like a Times Square billboard, but among the lights and quilted details of the Maybach, it’s just one more sparkly surface.

The screen is the main control center for all the electronic luxuries, which Maybach is equally generous about providing. Driver-assistance technologies include all the usual crash-avoidance systems and multi-view cameras, plus parking assist with wheel rim protection (something you’ll want if, like our car, your example has $1300 worth of 21-inch wheels). While the assists can feel overbearing, like a too-attentive waiter hovering over your table with the crumb scraper, the cameras and sensors make parking and maneuvering this massive car much less stressful.

At $291,600 as tested, the V-12 Maybach is not going to be on everyone’s shopping list, but in the elite scene of ultra-high-end taxicabs, it’s a bargain compared to offerings from marques like Rolls-Royce or Bentley. As a bold statement, the Maybach introduces your arrival loud and clear, from all 12 cylinders.

Like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them.   • This fresh food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.
  • It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.

This fresh food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.

It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.

Sources indicate that the new pyramid breaks away from the Trump administration’s updated nutritional guidelines, which are part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) agenda and prioritize red meat over plants.

The new pyramid was designed by a research team led by Brigham Young University professor Karen Della Corte. The researchers noted that this is the first international food pyramid that is designed to reflect scientific agreement across multiple countries and cultures.

Della Corte and researchers from the International Carbohydrate Quality Consortium (ICQC), compared dietary guidelines from multiple countries, including:.

They also analyzed evidence from more than 250 scientific publications, while drawing on the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet to identify principles of healthy eating that may be shared.

The upcoming pyramid highlights three guidelines:.

While the pyramid emphasizes plant-based proteins, it doesn’t exclude animal proteins.

“I find the fresh international food pyramid a more practical and aligned approach for the prevention of chronic disease,” stated Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the creation of the food pyramid.

“The fresh international food pyramid places greater emphasis on food quality and the importance of building meals around nutrient-dense plant foods, while still allowing room for lean animal proteins such as fish, poultry, eggs, and yogurt,” she added.

While the new pyramid and the current U.S. dietary guidelines differ in many ways, they also agree on certain factors.

For example, both sets of guidelines discourage added sugars, refined carbs, and highly processed snacks.

According to recent reports, the differences between the two mainly lie in their emphasis on specific sources of protein and fat. For example, the latest pyramid prioritizes plant-based proteins, while the U.S. guidelines place greater emphasis on animal proteins, including red meat.

Recent findings suggest that while both sets of recommendations advise limiting saturated fat, the new pyramid emphasizes unsaturated plant oils, whereas the U.S. guidelines also include butter and beef tallow as cooking fat options.

In a recent development, routhenstein noted that an key distinction is that this new pyramid goes beyond simply telling people to eat more protein or fewer carbohydrates. Instead, it encourages people to consider the quality and sources of those nutrients.

However, the main emphasis of both guidelines is encouraging people to eat fewer ultra-processed foods and more natural or “real” foods.

Routhenstein told Healthline that research consistently shows that plant-forward eating patterns, including the Mediterranean and DASH diets, are associated with better cardiovascular health and a lower risk of heart disease.

Plant foods provide fiber, potassium, antioxidants, and other beneficial compounds that can help support healthy cholesterol levels, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood vessel function.

“This is not to say that protein and fat are unimportant, but their sources matter,” Routhenstein said.

In a statement from BYU, Della Corte shared the following tips for incorporating the upcoming pyramid’s recommendations into your diet:.

It has been revealed that the pyramid is a framework, not a personalized prescription. If you have questions about your individual nutritional needs, you can speak with your healthcare professional or a licensed dietitian.

“It is important to recognize that plant-forward does not mean vegan or vegetarian. The amount and sources of animal protein should be considered to ensure they align with an individual’s cardiometabolic goals and lab targets,” Routhenstein stated.

Self-Affirmation, Self-Integrity, and You

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • It has been revealed that brief self-affirmation activities have been reliably shown to help people change and grow by reducing a perceived threat.
  • The vulnerability to stereotype threat we discussed in Part 1 of this series is grounded in a basic human need to see ourselves as “adaptively and morally adequate”: good, capable, reasonable and sensible people who are able to achieve the outcomes that matter to us.1 Named the self-integrity motive by Claude Steele, the psychologist who identified it,2 it differs from the better-known construct of self-esteem in that it is our motivation to view ourselves as “good enough,” rather than to maximize our positive thoughts and feelings about ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

This post is Part 2 of a series.

It has been revealed that brief self-affirmation activities have been reliably shown to help people change and grow by reducing a perceived threat. But what kind of threat do they reduce? And how does self-affirmation reduce it?

The vulnerability to stereotype threat we discussed in Part 1 of this series is grounded in a basic human need to see ourselves as “adaptively and morally adequate”: good, capable, reasonable and sensible people who are able to achieve the outcomes that matter to us.1 Named the self-integrity motive by Claude Steele, the psychologist who identified it,2 it differs from the better-known construct of self-esteem in that it is our motivation to view ourselves as “good enough,” rather than to maximize our positive thoughts and feelings about ourselves.

Our sense of self-integrity can be based on any valued qualities we believe we possess.3,4,5 Unfortunately, our self-integrity can also be threatened by anything we see as reflecting negatively on who we are: failure, bad things that happen to us, criticism or rejection, information that challenges what we believe, recognition that we’ve acted in ways that conflict with our values—any experience we take as evidence that we are bad, wrong, incompetent, irrational, foolish, or unable to deal effectively with life.

We feel bad about ourselves (ashamed, humiliated, unworthy) when our self-integrity is threatened, which triggers defensive efforts to protect or restore it: We may dismiss or minimize the threat; attack its source; marshal evidence against it; rationalize or justify our behavior, or deny being responsible for it; try to puff ourselves up through self-aggrandizing statements or comparing ourselves with people who we believe are worse.6,7,8 Any of these strategies may reestablish our self-integrity, but only temporarily—and they leave us vulnerable to more of the same kinds of threats.

Industry observers note that this is where self-affirmation can change the story. Focusing on important or valued aspects of the self that are not affected by the self-integrity threat bolsters our global sense of being “good enough”— protectively, if we self-affirm before we feel threatened, or restoratively, if we self-affirm afterward. It also makes all our defensive responses unnecessary, and in doing so promotes honest self-awareness and constructive responses to the challenges we face. Put simply, self-affirmation creates a protective buffer by putting the threat in perspective and helping us take a broader view of ourselves: Yes, I may have been wrong, made a bad decision, acted in a way I regret—but I’m a good and capable person, and my flaws and mistakes don’t define me.2,4,9.

The research on self-affirmation shows how it benefits us in concrete ways. Self-affirmation increases our acceptance of information about risks to our health that would otherwise feel threatening.10,11,12 It increases our openness to evidence that challenges dearly held beliefs, and decreases our tendency to evaluate arguments for and against those beliefs in favor of what we already believe.13,14 It reduces the mental energy spent ruminating on failures and flaws and frees our mental resources for more productive activities, improving performance under stress on tasks that require focused attention, problem-solving, creativity, and insight.9,15,16,17 It increases our self-compassion and fosters helping behavior toward others.18.

Recent findings suggest that most broadly, self-affirmation activities have consistently been shown to enhance the well-being of those who engage in them:9 It improves the general sense of feeling good, of having community and belonging; it offers relief from symptoms like depression and anxiety that create barriers to well-being; and it improves one's sense that they are a person of competence and value. And just as in the case of the studies of women dissatisfied with their weight that we began with in Part 1, these effects on well-being are long-lasting and get larger with the passage of time.

Can self-affirmation make a difference for you? Here’s an activity that will allow you to experience it for yourself. (For the most meaningful experience, please have paper and pen ready. And please do each of these steps in turn, waiting until you’ve finished the one you’re doing to go on to the next, rather than reading ahead to the end.).

1. Think of an area of your life that you have been struggling with. It could be a behavior you’ve been trying to change, but have not changed; something you’ve been wanting to do, but have not done; a decision you’ve been trying to make, but have not made. Once you identify it, please spend the next minute just thinking about the struggle and what it has been like for you.

Industry observers note that 2. From the following list, please choose one value that a) is very crucial to you, and has been important in your life, b) is not related to the area of your life you have been struggling with.

3. Think of a time when the value you chose was crucial to you. For the next few minutes, please write about that time and why that value was important to you.

Self-affirmation is most powerful when we’re facing a challenge of high personal importance, which is when our self-integrity is most likely to be threatened.19 Because self-affirmation works by focusing us on an aspect of ourselves that we feel good about and that does not feel threatened, it’s important to choose a value that’s unrelated to the challenge at hand; trying to affirm a threatened aspect of the self often makes us more defensive rather than less.19 And self-integrity is strengthened the most when we affirm “self-transcendent” values (values that express concern for others), rather than values that primarily benefit ourselves.4.

The positive effects of self-affirmation on how we feel and how we act reinforce a key tenet of motivational interviewing: we’re most likely to change and grow not when we feel sufficiently bad about ourselves, but when we feel accepted and valued.20 When you embark on a path toward change, don’t neglect to focus on what makes you worthy of value and respect just as you are.
