How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight.
  • In a recent development, that’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s.
  • “[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

In a recent development, that’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

It has been revealed that in healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic mentioned they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

It has been revealed that “People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” stated Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”.

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she stated.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing major rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” remarked Rowland.

At first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

Recent findings suggest that “[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she said. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”.

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland said.

Rowland remarked she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Firm, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland remarked she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” said Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she noted she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she said.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

In a recent development, “Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she said. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”.

In addition to medication, Rowland mentioned managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

It has been revealed that “Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she remarked. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”.

She said red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

It has been revealed that “Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” remarked Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”.

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she said.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

“[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” said Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”.

If you prefer to take baths, she said use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic noted to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.

  • According to recent reports, the seating position, which you can check out below, is but one of the unique selling points (or disqualifying features) of the Sanrivatti One.
  • According to recent reports, the chassis consists of a carbon fiber monocoque, while a double-wishbone pushrod suspension keeps the 2425-pound car in balance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s a fresh supercar organization out of the Netherlands that, apparently, thinks the orientation we typically sit in to drive is out of style. It asks, what if your head was forward of your legs? And, what if you were kneeling as opposed to sitting? Strange, yes—but now such a machine exists. The car in question is called the Sanrivatti One, and the Dutch startup just revealed all the details.

According to recent reports, the seating position, which you can check out below, is but one of the unique selling points (or disqualifying features) of the Sanrivatti One. All of the bits around the driver seem more likely to please folks. It has a mid-mounted 5.5-liter naturally aspirated Judd V-10 that makes 800 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque, and peak horsepower is produced at a beautiful 9000 rpm. There’s no electrification to be found, and all the power goes to the rear wheels via a Hewland six-speed sequential transmission.

According to recent reports, the chassis consists of a carbon fiber monocoque, while a double-wishbone pushrod suspension keeps the 2425-pound car in balance. (Mind you, that quoted weight is dry weight, so expect the final curb weight to be higher.) Braking is handled by AP Racing carbon discs with six-piston calipers in both front and rear. Sanrivatti fits Michelin slick tires from the factory, making it a track-only affair. Noted tires wrap 18-inch forged magnesium alloy wheels.

Acceleration figures aren’t available, but the Dutch organization claims a 205-mph top speed. Its funky design and aero helps that effort, as Sanrivatti says the exterior is inspired by both the peregrine falcon and a fighter jet. The falcon can be seen in the single sweeping character line that seems to mimic a falcon’s wing in a dive; meanwhile, the single-piece canopy and nose-positioned intakes aim to evoke the aircraft. There’s a large wing that rises up and out from the diffuser, and the majority of the rear is otherwise left open to help dissipate heat from that major V-10.

Meanwhile, here’s what the company has to say about that wild driving position. “Creating an exceptional hypercar is difficult enough,” says Paul Arkesden, executive director of technology partnerships at Sanrivatti. “Creating one around an entirely different driving position means rethinking the relationship between packaging, structure, aerodynamics, ergonomics and controls from the outset. That is what makes the One so interesting.”.

The final form of this seating position is similar to what you might experience on a motorcycle, so those who ride could find some familiarity there. Sanrivatti claims it offers about 3.2x better visibility than competitor supercars and track cars. And in case you were worried about being deeply uncomfortable (we sure are), Sanrivatti claims it’s developing “proprietary body-support and control technologies” that “allow the driver to move more naturally with the vehicle while remaining supported and secured.”.

While today marks the full public debut of the One, it’s still deep in testing stages, with track testing and prototype builds to come. There’s no target date for delivery as of now, so we’ll just need to wait and see what comes our way from Sanrivatti.

#17497. Be the Riverbank for Children’s Emotional Rivers

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1215 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Be the Riverbank for Children’s Emotional Rivers

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • “I used to yell at my daughter when she cried, to make her tougher.
  • According to recent reports, children’s emotions need to flow freely, like a river.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

“I used to yell at my daughter when she cried, to make her tougher. Even after I learned that crying is how she expresses herself when she has major emotions, I still yelled. I couldn’t deal with feeling helpless to make her happy again. Slowly, I learned that I have to take care of my own emotions and let my own tears out. Now when my daughter cries I cuddle with her, she lets out her tears, and we both feel better afterward. We call it cuddling the cry away.”.

According to recent reports, children’s emotions need to flow freely, like a river. That means parents need to be the riverbank. A riverbank safely contains the flow of feelings—preventing a flood—but doesn’t dam the flow by ignoring feelings, judging them, or forcing them to change. After all, a riverbank doesn’t decide how warm or cool the water in the river should be, or how fast or slow it should flow.

Parents who can express their own emotions in a healthy way can listen to children’s feelings without becoming overwhelmed by them. As a dad remarked to me recently, “I often tell my children something that I only learned recently for myself: If you are happy, you can laugh; if you are sad, you can cry.”.

The riverbank is the river’s home. Children need a safe physical home, and they also need a safe emotional home, often called the secure home base. This isn’t always easy for adults. It’s hard to sit with intense feelings in children, especially difficult ones like anger or grief.

Recent findings suggest that imagine two children who fight at a playground, and each goes running to their parent. One parent says, “Don’t come crying to me.” The other parent says, “Oh, poor baby, we will never come to this playground again. I’ll never let that mean child near you.” I see many instances of each extreme—dismissal of the child’s emotions or joining the child in emotional flooding.

In between is a good level of emotional support: “That looked like it hurt your body and your feelings. How did you try to solve the problem? How did that work? What else might you try next?”.

According to recent reports, if you can talk with both children, you might add: “Looks like you two are having some trouble. It’s hard when friends fight. Does anyone have any ideas on how to play together again?”.

It has been revealed that children need a safe place for the free flow of all their feelings, but a safe home base is especially relevant for sadness. When children feel sadness, loneliness, or loss, they need a place of warmth and love where they can heal from that pain.

Mabel was almost 3 when her parents began to talk to her about starting preschool. It would be her first time away from both parents for any extended period. She enjoyed her visit to the school, but asked her mother many times, “Will you be here with me?” When she understood that she would not be with her parents or grandparents at school, she lost her enthusiasm and was a bit sad.

In a recent development, mabel’s family understood that their job was to offer comfort and security, not to convince her it would be fun: “I understand that you’re sad. It’s hard to imagine having fun when you’ll miss your family.”.

A few days before school started, while her grandma gave her a bath, Mabel remarked to the little bath-toy animals, “You’re going to school.” Grandma picked up a toy and gave it a voice: “Will you be with me?” Mabel answered, taking on the role of the mother, “You’ll be by yourself.” Grandma had her animal say with worry, “Oh no!” Mabel responded gently, “Oh, it will be OK.” Then they made all the animals splash around in the water, with lots of laughter.

It has been revealed that this game provided Mabel with the ability to work through her sad feelings, and she made an excellent adjustment to preschool. Of course, she was sad sometimes when saying goodbye, but she knew she had a safe place at home to feel her sadness.

Recent findings suggest that it is inevitable that children will be sad at times. Children need to know that their parents can handle their heartbreak, without becoming so overwhelmed that they respond with anger or dismissal, such as: “Stop crying or I’ll leave you here all alone.” Sad children need to hear instead, “I’m here with you. This is very painful. Together we can hold this big feeling.” This may not make the sadness go away immediately. That’s not the goal. A mother confronted me at a workshop: “I listened to my son, like you said, and he was still sad.” Yes, it’s heartbreaking and true. Fortunately, it’s not a parent’s job to take away the feeling, but to sit with the child while the tears flow. The sadness will pass.

A mother recently shared with me an example of this new way of thinking about sadness:.

“The other day my daughter came back from the neighbor’s house crying. The other children did not play with her, and she felt very sad. I squatted down and hugged her. At the same time, my brain was thinking fast. How should I solve the problem for her? For a moment, I had nothing to say, so I repeated what she told me and looked at her. I gave her a hug and sympathized with her. She finished her tears and had good ideas for resolving these friendship problems the next time. The trouble was solved easily. Our emotional connection worked much better than my usual approach, which was to tell her what she should do. In this case, it was a very good thing that I couldn’t think of any so-called good ideas!”.

According to recent reports, it is time to stop seeing tears as a sign of weakness, especially in boys, who are expected to be tough from the very start of their lives. Many boys learn the “boy rules” and try to block all their tears from an early age. If they are “successful,” they are on the road to being emotionally constricted men. If they “fail,” they may be teased or bullied by other boys, or even by adults. This puts boys in an impossible position. The solution is for them to have safety at home, with parents, to let down their guard and let out their tears, even if they choose to hold them in sometimes with their peers. Boys are lucky if they know that someone sees them as OK no matter what they feel or how they show it. Boys are really lucky if they have adult men in their lives who are willing to accept tears, talk about emotions, and even cry themselves sometimes.

Children’s sadness needs to flow freely, with a loving adult sitting nearby or holding them close. Even the toughest kids (and grownups) have tears inside that need to come out.

#17495. Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.
  • According to recent reports, the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected.
  • Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator demonstrates today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

According to recent reports, the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator demonstrates today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.

It has been revealed that A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

On November 6, the same day Elon Musk unveiled the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

New inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search indicated no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

If there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

But the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”.

Industry observers note that that’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

Some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t stated whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

This is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

It has been revealed that I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we remarked it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

According to recent reports, if you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper newly introduced option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends.
  • It has been revealed that last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys).
  • “Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends. And yet that’s what happened at the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southeastern Pennsylvania, between a turkey and a mourning dove.

It has been revealed that last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys). To calm them down, the team put them with a feather-duster as a stand-in mother turkey. Because turkey poults are easily stressed, they are difficult to rehabilitate, according to a Facebook post by the wildlife center. In fact, one of them didn’t make it.

“Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote. “We paired it with a baby mourning dove of similar size, hoping they would comfort each other while eating and exploring as they are both ground eaters.”.

Sources indicate that the pairing turned out to be a raging success. They formed an inseparable bond that Raven Ridge Wildlife Center had never seen before. Months later, the team gave the dove a soft release, meaning the bird could leave whenever it wanted. But he clearly had no intention of leaving his friend. The dove continued returning to the turkey’s cage, and the two would sit near each other on either side of the separation.

Sources indicate that “After a few days, we put the dove back in with the turkey, and it was clear they were happiest together,” the wildlife center explained. But “we knew keeping them caged for the rest of their lives, or keeping them just because they were cute, was neither an option nor fair to these wild animals.”.

As such, the team contacted a large sanctuary in Pennsylvania to request a joint release. This way, the duo could choose whether to stick together or follow their own paths. After their soft release, the dove flew into the trees and the turkey started foraging, free to stick together or join other members of their species.

“We don’t know if they’ll stay together, but our team made sure they had a safe place until they were ready to be on their own,” the wildlife center concluded.

Former Rimac stakeholder Porsche once considered its own electric hypercar, only to pivot to an internal-combustion supercar instead. Even as cars like the Tesla Roadster and Yangwang U9 Xtreme make headlines with record-setting stunts, there are questions on whether or not a conventional hypercar buyer would be interested in paying for an EV.

Industry News: Intelligent Speed Limiter Company President: We Don’t Want Our Devices in Every Vehicle in America

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that michael Travars, president of active roadway safety technology tech giant LifeSafer, has worked for decades to save lives on the road.
  • Sources indicate that intelligent speed assistance devices have become a hot topic of discussion among municipal governments and car enthusiasts alike in recent years.
  • Sources indicate that “We don't want this in every car.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that michael Travars, president of active roadway safety technology tech giant LifeSafer, has worked for decades to save lives on the road. From ignition interlocks to intelligent speed limiters, Travars has spent his career piloting technology that reduces injuries and deaths in cars. But even this highly safety-conscious executive doesn’t believe in a statewide or federal speed limiter mandate.

Sources indicate that intelligent speed assistance devices have become a hot topic of discussion among municipal governments and car enthusiasts alike in recent years. The European Union mandated that all latest cars feature passive ISA systems, which acoustically alert drivers when they exceed the speed limit, in 2024. In the United States, states like New York and cities like Washington, D.C. are piloting programs that require so-called “super speeders” (who have been found guilty of extreme speeding) to install active ISA systems, which prevent lead-footed drivers from exceeding the limits altogether. LifeSafer is working closely with these municipalities to hone the technology—but Travars’s vision of expansion is somewhat limited.

Sources indicate that “We don't want this in every car. We actually don't want the European mandate of ISA in every single vehicle. There's a freedom of the road culture here. I'm a big believer in that,” Travars said to Road & Track. “We think a lot about the ignition interlock programs. The ignition interlock program reinforces that you don't drive drunk. It doesn't let you drive drunk. The theory behind those programs is that it creates a habit. You can't drive with alcohol. At the end of the program, the ignition interlock device comes out, and they go back to normal driving programs.”.

In a recent development, using the ISA device is fairly simple. A small screen is mounted on the dashboard, wired through the vehicle’s OBDII port, and operates with a GPS database of roadway speed limits. The device prevents the vehicle from exceeding the posted limit, with a programmable margin of a few miles per hour over said limit. Travars said the devices cost around $6 per day to operate. The device can be overridden, and it includes an RPM-limiting feature that softens typical acceleration.

“There's a tuning process. Actually, if you've done race car driving, it's a lot like tuning a race car, where you connect configuration tools. You actually put the car in neutral. You push the gas pedal all the way down. It measures the rate of acceleration,” Travars explained. “It is a calibration or a tuning process to do the install. And it's more than just OEM or model-specific. It's actually car-specific. A worn-down accelerator pedal has different movement than a modern accelerator, so it is absolutely a car-by-car process.”.

LifeSafer ISA right now has three primary customers: teens, fleets, and super speeders. Instead of merely monitoring teenage drivers through apps like Life360, some parents are taking action to limit the ability of their newly minted drivers to speed. Fleet operators enjoy similar benefits, including a theoretical increase in efficiency on speed-limited vehicles. But the future of the technology, arguably, is in providing compliance devices for governments.

Industry observers note that virginia has little tolerance for speeding, and the commonwealth was the first state to join forces with LifeSafer earlier this year. As of July 2026, certain reckless drivers are required to install an intelligent speed assistance device under the administration of the Commission on Virginia Alcohol Safety Action Program. And Virginia isn’t the only state in conversation with LifeSafer, either; Travars noted seven states—Hawaii, Illinois, Arizona, Maryland, New York, Virginia, and Georgia—have implemented super speeders laws, and around 17 states in total have reached out to the safety technology organization.

Industry observers note that but Travars stated he believes the state and city level should be the ceiling for these devices. While the safety technology industry would benefit from federal regulatory goalposts, Travars explained, the implementation of speed limiters is better suited to state-by-state needs.

“I would love to see federal minimum guidelines as to, what the device must do, how many miles it must be accurate for, a certification process; those kinds of things belong at the federal level. At the state level, what kind of program do you want? How long do you want it for? Who goes in it? Let Maryland do Maryland,” Travars remarked.

When asked why enthusiasts shouldn’t worry about ISA programs, Travars explained that driving culture in the United States differs greatly from Europe or other markets where widespread ISA programs have been implemented. These devices aren’t meant to limit drivers who have proven themselves to be responsible. Instead, LifeSafer wants these devices to be a temporary stop on the road to safer driving habits.

According to recent reports, “Active ISA devices are targeted programs specifically for drivers who need them. These are inexperienced drivers or drivers who have shown that they have a speeding habit that needs to be broken. Period. We don't want ISA in all vehicles. We don't want this to be a mandate in all cars. The goal is to take people who are unsafe drivers, make them safer, and then take them out of the program and restore their right to drive,” Travars said. “These aren't traps. These aren't the [devices] where they report to insurance companies to increase your rates. The data is not sold to third parties ... I think these programs should bar the right to sell that data. These are not trackers. These are not Big Brother. These are meant to serve a specific purpose, which is to reinforce safe driving behavior long enough that it becomes a habit. Full stop.”.

#17490. Industry News: Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What a Missed Deadline Taught Me About Switching Off

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (844 w)

Industry News: Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What a Missed Deadline Taught Me About Switching Off

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I missed a deadline last week.
  • In a recent development, the main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece.
  • The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

In a recent development, the main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Industry observers note that switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

It has been revealed that I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

According to recent reports, A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a massive screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on said little screen.

It has been revealed that regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an key thing to work on.

Recent findings suggest that A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Recent findings suggest that whatever the science says, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I remarked my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

With Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most vital thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

And if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Latest Update: 7 apps that really show what the fresh Apple iPhone Duo can do

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It took a while, but Apple has finally launched its first foldable: the iPhone Duo is now available in Star White or Night Sky finishes, starting at $1,999 and up, depending on how much storage you want inside.
  • Sources indicate that apple has built a variety of adaptations into iOS to support the iPhone Duo, so icons and menus will shift if the software detects it’s running on the inner or outer display of the foldable, rather than a standard iPhone.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re also seeing several apps built or optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo, to take advantage of that foldable screen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took a while, but Apple has finally launched its first foldable: the iPhone Duo is now available in Star White or Night Sky finishes, starting at $1,999 and up, depending on how much storage you want inside.

Sources indicate that apple has built a variety of adaptations into iOS to support the iPhone Duo, so icons and menus will shift if the software detects it’s running on the inner or outer display of the foldable, rather than a standard iPhone. In addition, iOS developers are updating their own apps to better suit the two newly introduced screen sizes introduced by the foldable.

Recent findings suggest that we’re also seeing several apps built or optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo, to take advantage of that foldable screen. Whether you’ve got the phone or not, they’re worth checking out as a showcase of what’s possible with the fresh form factor.

Toastie ($2.99) is a rather whimsical game for the iPad, iPhone, and iPhone Duo. The aim is to make the best grilled sandwich you can, and on Apple’s foldable phone you snap the handset shut and open it again to control the cooking time for your toasties.

Recent findings suggest that you can pick different ingredients and bread types as you go, and the ability to partially open the iPhone Duo to peek at your culinary creation is a nice touch. It’s not the most sophisticated cooking sim, but you might be surprised by how much fun it is to play.

Bring some old-school to your iPhone Duo with Tiny Computers ($3.99): With the foldable half open and propped up, the flat half turns into a virtual keyboard, and the vertical half shows a simulated display from a classic computer of your choice—with 10 to pick from.

The available computers include vintage Windows and Mac machines, plus the Commodore 64; while these aren’t full-scale emulators, you can play around with them and discover some “nostalgic secrets” as you go (including some iconic keyboard sounds).

It has been revealed that there are also gaming experiences specifically for the iPhone Duo to enjoy. Marbles Unhinged (freemium, $2.99 to unlock all levels) is a marble-rolling game that uses your phone’s accelerometer and gyroscope to create realistic physical tilting controls.

Recent findings suggest that with the iPhone Duo half open, one half of the main display becomes the marble maze, and the other half becomes a ramp you use to get the marble moving to the right place at the right speed. There are 10 levels available to play for free before you have to pay.

Simply put, Foldissimo (free, $9.99 to unlock all the songs) turns your iPhone Duo into a virtual accordion. You can adjust the airflow affecting the instrument by folding and unfolding the Apple device—faster folds pump in more air and increase the volume.

Recent findings suggest that there is a selection of classic song tutorials included to get you started, and you can compose your own too. You can also switch to other instruments, including panpipes and a theremin, but that’ll cost you extra. A clever idea, neatly implemented.

If you’ve got a hankering for the days when we carried camcorders around as separate gadgets—rather than just using our phones to record video—then Flipcorder ($4.99) is a perfect iPhone Duo app, complete with a retro-looking interface and workflow.

According to recent reports, you can only record videos in 20-second bursts, up to 30 minutes a day, reflecting the limitations of camcorders of yesteryear. When you close the foldable, the outer display shows your subjects what’s being filmed, which is a smart touch. (And don’t forget to back your videos up.).

In a recent development, if you remember the Walkman era, then you’ll love Deck-Man ($4.99), which gives the iPhone Duo the feel of a classic cassette player. It interfaces with Apple Music and any music files you’ve got stored locally on your device to give audio playback a retro feel.

Your albums show up as cassette tapes, and there are chunky virtual buttons for starting and stopping the audio—with the familiar fast forward, rewind, and eject buttons here too. The app even includes authentic mechanical sounds, recorded from a real cassette player.

Industry observers note that unfold Your City (free; $4.99 to unlock all the cities) utilizes the iPhone Duo’s foldable form factor to turn the handset into a virtual pop-up book that serves as your guide to the world’s most famous cities. You can even switch between day and night modes.

It’s a fresh twist on the usual travel guide format, and plenty of care and attention has been put into the details here (nice touches include a Tower Bridge that actually opens in London). Be warned, though: the app may have a serious impact on your travel budget.

BYD's Futuristic EV Charger Can Run On Sunshine And Batteries

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that BYD has already shown that charging an EV doesn’t have to take much longer than filling a gas tank.
  • Industry observers note that its new site in the Abu Dhabi desert combines solar panels, battery storage, Flash Charging, and a robotic arm that plugs in the car.
  • It has been revealed that battery-backed charging is becoming more common because it lets stations deliver more power than their grid connection alone can supply, while also reducing demand on the grid during busy periods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that BYD has already shown that charging an EV doesn’t have to take much longer than filling a gas tank. Now it’s tackling another problem: getting enough electricity to a fast charger in the first place.

Industry observers note that its new site in the Abu Dhabi desert combines solar panels, battery storage, Flash Charging, and a robotic arm that plugs in the car. BYD says the system can work independently of the electricity grid, potentially bringing fast charging to places where a power connection may not be feasible. The proposition is pretty simple: Solar panels generate electricity, batteries store it, and the charger sends it to an EV.

It has been revealed that battery-backed charging is becoming more common because it lets stations deliver more power than their grid connection alone can supply, while also reducing demand on the grid during busy periods. Tesla’s biggest Supercharger site, which it opened earlier this year, also uses solar panels and Tesla's Megapack batteries. Companies like Electric Era and Beam Global specialize in battery-backed charging. Even BYD Flash chargers not located in the middle of the desert and not supplied by solar panels use on-site energy storage to boost power delivery.

Sources indicate that each of BYD's T-shaped Flash chargers is hooked up to two 185-kilowatt-hour storage batteries, for 370 kWh total. These draw power from the grid at around 100 to 560 kilowatts, then supply the car at a much higher rate. The chargers can send up to 1,500 kW through one cable, or up to 1,000 kW when both are in use at the same time.

Adding solar panels into the equation means some or even all of that electricity can be generated on-site. However, BYD hasn’t disclosed the battery capacity or solar output of this newly introduced desert installation. So it's not clear how many cars the station can charge—or how swiftly—on solar power alone.

It has been revealed that the charging hardware is impressively quick. With BYD’s latest 1,500-kW Flash chargers, compatible cars running its second-generation Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or hit 97% in nine minutes.

Now that infrastructure is going global. The organization says it aims to establish 6,000 Flash Charging stations worldwide by the end of 2027, but it hasn’t specified how many will offer solar power, off-grid operation, or that robotic arm.

Industry observers note that europe is getting a taste of BYD’s Flash charging with sites up and running in Italy, Germany, France, and the United Kingdom. Canada is coming soon too. The only vehicle it currently sells in Europe that can fully utilize its power is the Denza Z9 GT. During a demonstration, the electric wagon charged from 10% to 80% in six minutes and 32 seconds, reaching 97% in nine minutes and 22 seconds.
